title: Preferred luminous conditions in open-plan offices: research and practice recommendations
authors: Veitch, J. A.; Newsham, G. R., 2001
research_question: To characterize preferred luminous conditions in open-plan offices, compare them to existing recommended practice and empirical data, and derive practical recommendations for lighting installations.

participants.description: 42 men and 52 women, age range 18-58 years, participated in age- and sex-matched pairs, in a one-day session, in Ottawa, Canada. Data from 26 participants were excluded due to English language skills or age-matching issues.
participants.recruitment: Participants were recruited for an experiment concerning individual control over lighting.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A windowless, 83 m² (880 ft²), open-plan office space containing six workstations (two rows of three), each 6 m² (65 ft²) defined by 1.67 m (66 in) partitions. The facility was outfitted with three dimmable lighting circuits: (1) two rows of five recessed 1' x 4' parabolic-louvered luminaires (centre), (2) two rows of five recessed 1' x 4' parabolic-louvered luminaires (perimeter), (3) eight furniture-mounted indirect luminaires on partitions. Two central workstations also had one non-dimmable undershelf task light. All lamps were 3500K and 80 CRI.

measures.construct: Log ratio of maximum to minimum luminance (40-degree field of view)
Percentage of black VDT screen with luminance >40 cd/m² (glare spot area)
Average luminance of points in black VDT screen with luminance > 40 cd/m² (glare spot luminance)

findings.mechanism: Participants chose conditions that they preferred for VDT office work, resulting in a wide range of desktop illuminance levels.
findings.quote: Luminous conditions in this investigation demonstrate wide individual variability. Desktop illuminance, for instance, varied from 83-725 lx.

findings.consequent: Compliance with IESNA RP-1 recommended illuminance (500 lx)
findings.mechanism: Over 60% of participants chose illuminance levels lower than the upper limit of IESNA RP-1 recommendations, consistent with other investigations.
findings.quote: Over 60% of participants chose illuminance levels lower than 500 lx, which is in keeping with the results of other investigations.

findings.mechanism: Participants' choices resulted in energy-efficient lighting, with mean LPD lower than current North American energy code maximums.
findings.quote: Mean lighting power density was 14.3 W/m² (SD=4.1), which is notable for being lower than present-day North American energy code maximum prescriptions

findings.mechanism: Participants chose a wide range of average luminances, with the median falling within CIBSE LG7 recommendations but lower than IESNA RP-1.
findings.source: Table 5, 3.1.3. Luminances in the field of view
findings.quote: The average luminance in the field of view was highly variable, ranging from 11.5 to 61.0 cd/m²... The median value, 39.2 cd/m²

findings.consequent: Log ratio of maximum to minimum luminance (LMM) in 40-degree field-of-view band
findings.mechanism: The preferred luminous conditions for office work might not create the most 'interesting' scene, as the median LMM was lower than Loe et al.'s most interesting scene.
findings.source: Table 5, 3.1.3. Luminances in the field of view
findings.quote: Our median LMM score (2.96) was far below the score for the most interesting scene of the set studied by Loe et al.(16)

findings.mechanism: The degree of desirable luminance variation might be greater than current recommendations, with chosen ratios ranging from 11:1 to 68:1.
findings.source: 3.1.3. Luminances in the field of view
findings.quote: In the present study, participants' maximum:minimum luminance ratios in the 40-degree band range from 11:1 through 68:1.

findings.mechanism: Participants sought to minimize the difference between VDT screen luminance and partitions, resulting in a lower ratio than IESNA/CIBSE limits.
findings.source: 3.1.3. Luminances in the field of view
findings.quote: The median preferred desk-to-partition luminance ratio (for this study, calculated using ID: Iave), 1.7:1, is lower than the 3:1 ratio limit

findings.mechanism: Participants sought to minimize the difference between VDT screen luminance and partitions, especially with dark characters on a light background.
findings.source: 3.1.3. Luminances in the field of view
findings.quote: The VDT-to-partition ratio is even smaller, 0.82:1

findings.antecedent: Time of lighting choice (morning by LC group vs. end of day by NC group)
findings.consequent: Size of reflected image glare on VDT (VDTG%)
findings.mechanism: NC participants, having worked all day, learned to ameliorate imperfect aspects of their lighting situations, leading to choices that created less VDT-screen glare.
findings.quote: NC participants chose levels lower than the LC participants (Table 7).

findings.antecedent: Time of lighting choice (morning by LC group vs. end of day by NC group)
findings.mechanism: NC participants, having worked all day, learned to ameliorate imperfect aspects of their lighting situations, leading to choices that resulted in lower LPD.
findings.quote: NC participants' lighting choices had lower average luminance of reflected images in the VDT screen and lower LPD.

findings.antecedent: Time of lighting choice (morning by LC group vs. end of day by NC group)
findings.mechanism: NC participants, having worked all day, learned to ameliorate imperfect aspects of their lighting situations, leading to choices that resulted in lower cylindrical illuminance.
findings.quote: These were for the size of reflected image glare on the VDT (VDTG%) and the cylindrical illuminance (Ecl). The pattern was maintained: in both cases, the NC participants chose levels lower than the LC participants (Table 7).

findings.mechanism: Age did not influence lighting choices in this investigation, consistent with some literature.
findings.quote: Age and sex did not influence lighting choices in this investigation.

findings.quote: Age and sex did not influence lighting choices in this investigation.

findings.mechanism: Despite diverse luminous conditions, participants reported high satisfaction, confirming that a wide range of conditions can satisfy people.
findings.quote: The ratings of lighting quality were very high (overall median 4.1 on a scale from 1-5, where higher values reflect better quality)

findings.mechanism: Despite diverse luminous conditions, participants reported high satisfaction, confirming that a wide range of conditions can satisfy people.
findings.quote: as were the environmental satisfaction ratings (median 3 on a scale 0-4).

findings.mechanism: Participants reported low bothersome glare, confirming that direct glare was not problematic with their chosen conditions.
findings.quote: Ratings of bothersome glare were low (median 1.8 on a scale 1-5).

findings.consequent: Preference for working in offices with windows
findings.mechanism: Window preferences are well-known and consistently reported.
findings.quote: Participants reported a strong preference for having a window

findings.antecedent: Environmental feature: presence of blinds or curtains with windows
findings.consequent: Preference for having a blind or curtain on the window
findings.mechanism: Participants desire control over daylight and privacy.
findings.quote: generally would want a blind or curtain on the window (items 1 and 2).

findings.antecedent: Environmental feature: electric lighting in presence of daylight
findings.consequent: Preference for electric lighting to supplement natural daylight
findings.mechanism: Recognition of the need for adequate light levels and quality beyond what daylight alone provides.
findings.quote: Over 50%, however, also wanted electric lighting to supplement natural daylight (item 9).

findings.consequent: Preference for a uniformly bright room to work in
findings.mechanism: A preference for consistent, predictable luminous environments.
findings.quote: The majority of participants reported a preference for a uniformly bright room to work in (57.4% reporting scores of 3 or 4, item 3).

findings.antecedent: Lighting condition: dark ambient levels with task lighting
findings.consequent: Preference for dark ambient levels and task lighting
findings.mechanism: This preference is not universal, contrasting with the 'light the walls, hide the sources' credo.
findings.quote: Only 17 % reported a preference for dark ambient levels and task lighting (item 4).

findings.consequent: Preference for working in a very dark room
findings.mechanism: This preference is not universal, contrasting with the 'light the walls, hide the sources' credo.
findings.quote: Even fewer (7.5%) reported a preference for working in a dark room (item 5).

findings.consequent: Perceived importance of lighting in offices
findings.mechanism: Lighting matters to the ordinary occupant, at least at a basic level.
findings.quote: A large majority of participants reported that lighting in their offices is important to them (item 6)

findings.mechanism: Individual control over lighting is important for occupant satisfaction and preference.
findings.quote: The ability to control office lighting is also important to most participants: 81% reported wanting to adjust the lights

findings.antecedent: Ability to change position or angle of lights
findings.consequent: Desire to change position or angle of lights
findings.mechanism: Individual control over lighting is important for occupant satisfaction and preference.
findings.quote: 69.2 % reported wanting to change position or angle of lights

findings.antecedent: Ability to turn lights on or off
findings.consequent: Desire to turn lights on or off during workday
findings.mechanism: Individual control over lighting is important for occupant satisfaction and preference.
findings.quote: 78.5 % wanted to be able to turn lights on or off during the workday

findings.mechanism: Preference for indirect lighting, though the question did not specify if it was alone or in combination with direct illumination.
findings.quote: Indirect lighting was desired by 46.8% of participants in this study.

findings.mechanism: NC participants reported that lighting was more important to them, but this was identified as an artifact of the skewness in the data and experimental manipulation.
findings.quote: Participants in the NC group reported that lighting was more important to them... The former effect, ratings of lighting importance, is an artifact of the skewness in the data.

findings.consequent: Desire to adjust lighting during the workday
findings.mechanism: LC participants reported a stronger desire to be able to adjust lighting during the workday, but this was identified as an artifact of the experimental manipulation.
findings.quote: LC participants reported a stronger desire to be able to adjust lighting during the workday. Both effects are artifacts.

mechanisms: Occupant preference for luminous conditions can identify the conditions that will satisfy human needs.
Participants sought to minimise the difference between the VDT screen luminance and the partitions, to avoid creating the effect of a bright luminous object against a dark field.
Participants learned through their day's experience how to ameliorate imperfect aspects of their lighting situations.
A wide range of conditions can satisfy people.
Individual control over lighting is important for occupant satisfaction and preference.
moderators: Time of lighting choice (morning vs. end of day)
implementation_implications: Provide the opportunity to adjust or change lighting at will to suit individual preferences, using controls that permit the creation of luminous conditions across a range of preferences.
Implement a mixture of direct and indirect ambient lighting, with approximately 40% being indirect.
Aim for desktop illuminances in the range specified by current recommended practice for VDT office lighting, acknowledging some individuals may prefer higher levels (up to 725 lx).
Design for a moderate degree of visual interest, represented by maximum to minimum luminance ratios in the visual field (40-degree band) on the order of 20:1 (LMM≈3).
Ensure ratios of average luminance between VDT and vertical surfaces in the visual field are rather uniform, especially when VDT screens with light backgrounds are used.
Design for very low or no reflected luminaire images in VDT screens, even with light-background screens.
Include a window, preferably with a blind, in office designs.

Further reductions in allowable lighting power densities will likely require improvements in lighting system energy efficiency, rather than changes in lighting design that could lead to unacceptable luminance patterns.

limitations: High intercorrelations between photometric variables complicate their use as independent predictors in multivariate analyses.
The camera geometry used for maximum ceiling luminance measurements did not permit calculating standard glare indices, limiting comparability with guidelines.
A general preference question about indirect lighting did not specify if it was desired alone or in combination with direct illumination, making comparison with actual choices difficult.
Some reported group differences (e.g., lighting importance, desire to adjust) were identified as artifacts of the experimental manipulation or data skewness.
The wide variability in preferred conditions among individuals makes it challenging to identify single optimal lighting conditions that satisfy everyone.
